name: Glycogen Storage Disease

criteria.description: Demonstration of deficient activity of specific glycogen-metabolizing enzyme in liver, muscle, or other tissues
Identification of pathogenic mutation(s) in genes associated with glycogen storage disease
Presence of characteristic clinical features such as hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, or muscle weakness
Histological evidence of abnormal glycogen accumulation in biopsy specimens

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Definitive diagnosis requires demonstration of enzyme deficiency or identification of pathogenic genetic mutation; clinical and histopathological findings support diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Subtypes of GSD require specific enzyme or genetic testing for accurate classification.

pathognomonic.notes: Enlarged liver is a hallmark in most GSD types
searchTerms: liver swelling due to stored sugar

pathognomonic.notes: Characteristic metabolic disturbance in hepatic forms
searchTerms: severe low blood sugar when fasting
fatigue and muscle weakness on activity

common.symptomName: Growth retardation or failure to thrive

common.notes: Due to impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
Progressive liver damage in some GSD types
Noted in certain subtypes such as GSD type II

occasional.notes: May cause aminoaciduria and electrolyte imbalances

searchTerms: high uric acid and gout attacks
elevated uric acid causing joint pain

occasional.notes: Resulting from recurrent low blood glucose
searchTerms: seizures caused by low blood sugar

rare.notes: Benign liver tumors with risk of malignant transformation

laboratory: Hypoglycemia with elevated lactate and uric acid
imaging: Hepatomegaly on abdominal ultrasound or CT
genetic: Pathogenic variants in genes such as G6PC, PYGM, AGL, and others depending on subtype
other: Muscle or liver biopsy showing excessive glycogen deposits
Enzyme activity assays confirming deficient glycogen metabolism

redFlags: Severe recurrent hypoglycemia causing seizures or coma
Rapidly progressive hepatomegaly with liver dysfunction
references: Rake JP et al. Glycogen storage disease type I: diagnosis, management, clinical course and outcome. Eur J Pediatr. 2002.
Chen M et al. Glycogen storage diseases: clinical and molecular aspects. Clin Genet. 2018.
commonPitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as idiopathic hypoglycemia in infants and children.
Hepatomegaly may be attributed to other causes such as viral hepatitis or fatty liver disease.
Muscle weakness may be mistaken for muscular dystrophy or other myopathies.
Failure to recognize fasting intolerance as a key feature.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: Glycogen storage diseases present with fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, but do not cause severe symptoms after fructose ingestion as seen in hereditary fructose intolerance.
Glycogen storage diseases often have hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycemia, while mitochondrial myopathies typically lack hepatomegaly and present with lactic acidosis and exercise intolerance.
Glycogen storage diseases present in childhood with hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, whereas fatty liver disease is more common in adults and lacks fasting hypoglycemia.

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of hypoglycemia during fasting excludes most hepatic forms of GSD.
Normal liver size and function tests in a symptomatic child make GSD unlikely.
No evidence of abnormal glycogen accumulation on tissue biopsy rules out GSD.
